title: Unsupervised seismic clustering reveals distinct drainage signals at Gornergletscher
summary: An unsupervised analysis of five weeks of seismic records from Gornergletscher, Switzerland, separated cryoseismic signals into clusters associated with the 2007 Gornersee lake flood and with afternoon/evening meltwater flow. One high-energy, broadband noise cluster began about two days before the reported onset of subglacial flooding; the authors suggest it captures the earlier initiation of englacial and subglacial drainage and improves the flood chronology.
ai_technology: SpecUFEx unsupervised feature extraction: non-negative matrix factorization, hidden Markov modeling, principal component analysis, and k-means clustering
organization: Columbia University; ETH Zurich; Swiss Federal Institute for Forest, Snow and Landscape Research (WSL)

evidence.tested: An unsupervised analysis of five weeks of seismic records from Gornergletscher, Switzerland, separated cryoseismic signals into clusters associated with the 2007 Gornersee lake flood and with afternoon/evening meltwater flow.
evidence.unknown: The analysis covers five weeks at one glacier using the 2007 flood record. The inferred drainage start precedes lake-level evidence by about two days, but the source cannot definitively exclude ice-bed slip, till deformation, or small fractures as explanations for some spectral features. The study interprets cluster timing and spectra as hydrologic signals; it does not directly image subglacial drainage pathways.
evidence.ai_role: The unsupervised learning pipeline reduced seismic spectrograms to fingerprints and grouped similar continuous-noise and icequake signals without labels. Comparing the learned clusters with lake level, GPS, temperature, and event timing exposed distinct clusters associated with lake-flood drainage and daily meltwater flow, which supported the revised drainage chronology.
